King County house prices: analysis and model report

Exploratory analysis, feature engineering, model comparison, tuning, and interpretation for house sale prices in King County, Washington (the Seattle area).

Source audit: 21,613 records. EDA population: 21,613 retained records. Target: price. Displayed subsets are labeled.

  • Data. 21,613 house sales in King County, Washington (the Seattle area) from May 2014 to May 2015, across 70 ZIP codes. The median price is $450,000 and the mean $540,088; price is strongly right-skewed (skewness 4.0), so models work on its logarithm.
  • Result. The final XGBoost predicts a sale price with a median error of 8.0% ($35,668) and is within 20% for 84% of unseen sales; RMSE is $131,898 because a few large sales dominate it. The median-price baseline has a median error of 34.4%.
  • Drivers. Location features account for 44% of the model's attributions, size for 33%, and grade for 10%. The three most influential features are zip_te, sqft_living, lat.
  • Where it is weaker. Error is highest for the cheapest homes (median 15.1%) and lowest in decile 5 (6.8%).
  • Tuning. Tuning the three tree models by random search (20 settings each) gave test median errors of Random forest 8.5% to 8.6%; Gradient boosting (gbm) 8.8% to 8.1%; XGBoost 8.5% to 8.0% (default to tuned); XGBoost won on cross-validated RMSE of log1p price.
  • Model families. With default settings, Random forest had the lowest cross-validated median absolute error ($38,184) and Ridge the highest ($48,771). The best tree-based model reaches $38,184 and the best linear model $46,696.

The sections that follow give the evidence: data, exploration, features, method, results, tuning, the final model and its interpretation, limitations, and how to reproduce the run.

Data quality, distributions, and dependence

3. Exploratory data analysis

The price distribution, every column, relationships with price, price by location, age and quality, collinearity, and the main insights.

Shape, skewness, and outliers of the target

3.1 Price distribution

Price is strongly right-skewed: a few very expensive sales stretch the raw scale, while log(price) is close to symmetric. Skewness measures this lopsidedness (0 is symmetric, positive is a long right tail) and excess kurtosis measures how heavy the tails are compared with a normal curve; the formulas are in the panel on the right. Working on the log scale makes equal steps equal percentage changes, which tames the skew so that a handful of sales no longer dominate averages and model fits. The Q-Q plot sorts log prices against what a normal curve would give, so bends at its ends show heavy tails. Tukey fences use the IQR, the spread of the middle 50% of prices (third quartile minus first quartile), to flag unusual values without assuming any distribution shape, a simple first screen for sales worth inspecting; flagged sales are not removed.

Correlation, heatmap, and key scatterplots

3.3 Relationships with price

Correlation of each feature with price, the full pairwise heatmap, and scatterplots of the six most price-correlated features. Pearson correlation measures straight-line association on the raw values. Spearman correlation applies the same idea to the ranks of the values, so the skew and outliers in price do not distort it and it also picks up steady curved relations; showing both is useful because a Spearman value clearly above the Pearson value means the relation is steady but curved or blunted by outliers. The orange lines in the scatterplots are smooth trend curves: they show the shape of the relation without assuming a straight line. Outlined heatmap cells mark pairs with a correlation above 0.40 in absolute value; strongly correlated features share information and motivate the VIF check in section 3.5. Coverage: price plus 15 numeric features. Excluded: id (an identifier, 21,436 distinct values across 21,613 records), date (sales span 13 months), zipcode (categorical), and lat and long, which are shown on the map in section 3.4.

3.4 Price by location, year built, and quality

3.5 Multicollinearity (VIF)

The correlation heatmap shows that several area and room-count features move together. VIF measures how much of each feature is explained by the others; checking it before interpreting coefficients matters because redundant features make estimates unstable (5 or more suggests notable collinearity, 10 or more severe). Living area equals above-ground plus basement area in every retained record, so those three are exactly dependent; the second panel removes living area to show the remaining collinearity. Coverage: the 15 numeric features are the predictors checked here; price is the target and is left out. Not covered: id, date, zipcode, lat, and long. The neighbour areas (sqft_living15, sqft_lot15) are expected to track the home's own areas. ZIP code is categorical, and this numeric VIF cannot show its overlap with the coordinates; that would need a generalized VIF on dummy-coded categories.

What the exploration shows

3.6 Key insights

The main findings from the sections above. Every number is computed from the retained records.

  • Price is extremely right-skewed, so model it on the log scale. Skewness is 4.0 on the raw scale and 0.43 after taking logs. The mean ($540,088) sits 20% above the median ($450,000). Log price is close to symmetric, although its tails are still heavier than a normal curve (excess kurtosis 0.7).
  • A handful of very expensive sales dominate raw-scale statistics. 1,146 sales lie above the raw Tukey fence ($1,129,575); on the log scale 281 lie above and 52 below the fences ($113,535 to $1,829,012). The most expensive sale is $7,700,000 for 12,050 sq ft in ZIP 98102 ($639 per sq ft against a median of $245); the cheapest is $75,000 for 670 sq ft in ZIP 98022. Large prices are plausible for large, high-grade homes, so these sales stay in the data and are flagged, not removed.
  • Size and build quality matter most among the numeric features. Spearman correlation with price: Grade 0.66, Living area 0.64, Nearby living area 0.57, Above-ground area 0.54. Compare the Pearson columns in the chart: the Pearson correlation of living area is 0.70 with log price and 0.70 with raw price. Lot area, Nearby lot area, Condition show almost no monotone relation with price (absolute Spearman correlation below 0.10).
  • Location and grade each explain a large share of price. ZIP code alone explains 52.8% of the variance in log price (adjusted R-squared), and grade alone 49.7%. Among the 70 ZIP codes with at least 20 sales, the median price runs from $235,000 (ZIP 98002) to $1,892,500 (ZIP 98039), a ratio of 8.1 (highest over lowest). The map shows the pattern: the highest prices cluster around Lake Washington and the Eastside, and the lowest in the south of the county.
  • Year built is weakly and non-monotonically related to price, and it is entangled with size. Median price is $474,000 to $550,000 for homes built before 1940, falls to $379,975 in the 1960s, and is $486,388 to $539,950 from the 1990s on. Median living area ranges from 1,370 sq ft (1940s) to 2,450 (2010s), while price per square foot falls from $351 for the 1900s to $215 for the 1960s.
  • Grade, waterfront, and view separate prices more than condition does. Median price is $375,000 for grade 7 (8,981 sales), $720,000 for grade 9 and $1,284,000 for grade 11. For condition it is $450,000 at 3, $440,000 at 4, $526,000 at 5; conditions 1 and 2 cover only 202 sales, too few to read. The 163 waterfront sales have a median of $1,400,000 against $450,000; homes with the best view (4) have $1,185,000 against $432,500 with no view.
  • Living area is exactly above-ground plus basement area. Those three features cannot all enter a regression. After dropping sqft_living the largest VIF is 4.83 (section 3.5).

Model inputs without leakage

4. Feature engineering

How the raw columns become model inputs, which rows are touched and why, and how each step avoids leaking held-out information. The numbers come from scripts/run_features.R, which writes the CSV files this section reads.

Rules and the rows they affect

4.1 Data quality rules

Every rule says how many rows it touches, and nothing is removed silently. The only rows ever excluded are the sales with a non-positive price, which cannot be log-transformed. Price per square foot catches sales whose price does not fit their size; such rows are left out of model fitting inside each fold, never out of evaluation.

RuleRows affectedWhat we do
Missing cells in the source file0Nothing to impute. A median imputer stays in every pipeline as a guard and is fitted on training rows only.
Sales with a non-positive price0None found, so none removed. Any such row would be excluded because it cannot be log-transformed.
Exact duplicate rows0None found, so none removed.
Rows sharing a property id with another row (resales)353Kept: repeat sales are valid observations. Cross-validation folds are grouped by property so a house never sits in both training and test.
More than 10 bedrooms2Kept and flagged: an implausible entry, but a single row cannot move the models.
Build year later than the sale year12Kept: the house was sold before completion. Its age is negative, which is a valid signal for a new build.
Renovation year later than the sale year6Kept: the renovation was recorded after the sale. last_update_year uses it as recorded.
Zero bedrooms and zero bathrooms7Kept and flagged because the combination is unusual, not proven wrong (for example an unfinished or unusual unit).
Renovation year earlier than build year0None found, so none changed. last_update_year would take the later of the two years anyway.
Living area differs from above-ground plus basement0None found. The three areas are still exactly dependent in the other direction, which the ridge penalty absorbs.
Price per sq ft in the lowest 1% or highest 1% of a fold's training rows278 of 13,828 training rows per fold (2.0%)Left out of model fitting only, inside each fold, because a few extreme sales can pull the model away from typical homes. Held-out rows are never trimmed, and the comparison below fits with and without trimming.

What is built and where it is fitted

4.2 Location and engineered features

Location enters in two ways. The file has coordinates, so set E adds latitude, longitude, and the great-circle distance to downtown Seattle and to downtown Bellevue; these are computed from each row alone, so they cannot leak. ZIP code is encoded as well, and these encodings are fitted on training rows only: a target encoding of ZIP (the smoothed average log price of the ZIP's training sales, shrunk toward the overall average for ZIPs with few sales), and a hot-ZIP flag with a four-level price tier (hot means the top fifth of ZIPs that have at least 10 training sales). ZIP codes unseen or too rare in training get the average tier and no hot flag. The final pipeline uses set E, which had the lowest cross-validated error: the ZIP encoding gives the neighbourhood level and the distances add a smooth measure of position.

FeatureHow it is builtWhere it is fittedUsed in setsWhy
log_living, log_lotNatural log of living and lot areaRow-wise (no fitting)B, C, D, EAreas are right-skewed; logs make their effect closer to proportional
has_basement, renovated1 if basement area or renovation year is above zeroRow-wise (no fitting)B, C, D, ETurns zero-means-none codes into explicit flags
ageSale year minus build year (negative for homes sold before completion)Row-wise (no fitting)B, C, D, EEasier to read than a calendar year
last_update_yearThe later of the build year and the renovation year (a new column)Row-wise (no fitting)B, C, D, EResolves renovation years that precede the build year
bath_per_bedBathrooms divided by bedrooms (bedrooms floored at 1)Row-wise (no fitting)B, C, D, ECaptures amenity level independent of size
ZIP target encodingSmoothed mean log1p price of the ZIP's training sales, shrunk toward the overall mean for small ZIPs; cross-fitted so a training row never sees its own priceFitted on training rows of each foldC, D, ETurns 70 ZIP codes into one informative number
zip_hot1 if the ZIP is in the top fifth of ZIPs (at least 10 training sales) by mean log1p priceFitted on training rows of each foldDMarks the expensive core areas
zip_tierPrice quartile (0 to 3) of the ZIP's training mean; unseen or rare ZIPs get the overall mean's tierFitted on training rows of each foldDCoarse, robust location ranking
lat, long, dist_seattle_km, dist_bellevue_kmCoordinates as recorded, plus great-circle (haversine) distance in km to downtown Seattle and downtown BellevueRow-wise (no fitting)EPrices fall with distance from the job centres, and ZIP codes are coarse; row-wise, so no leakage
ScalingNumeric inputs standardized with training-fold mean and spreadFitted on training rows of each foldRidge onlyLinear models need comparable scales; trees do not

Log1p target, scored in dollars

4.3 Target transform and metrics in USD

Price is modeled as log1p(price) inside the fitting pipeline, the R counterpart of scikit-learn's TransformedTargetRegressor: the pipeline log-transforms the target for fitting and inverts predictions with expm1 before scoring, so every figure below is in US dollars on the original scale (RMSE log1p is shown only to connect with the log-scale results earlier). Dollar RMSE is dominated by a few very expensive sales, so MAE, the median percentage error and the share of predictions within 20% are shown next to it. Scores come from 5-fold cross-validation grouped by property on the 17,285 development sales; the other 4,328 are the hold-out set described in the next subsection.

Reading the table (bold marks the best value per column): adding ZIP target encoding (set C) is the biggest single step. It cuts the median percentage error from 18.1% (set B) to 10.2% for XGBoost and from 20.1% to 12.2% for Ridge. The hot-ZIP flag and price tier (set D) change the median error by 0.01 points for XGBoost and -0.19 for Ridge on top of the encoding, so the simpler encoding is enough. Row-wise engineered features (set B) move the median error by -0.71 points for Ridge and -0.11 for XGBoost relative to the raw features (set A). Trimming outliers from the fitting rows changes little: XGBoost on set D reaches 10.2% with trimming and 10.1% without. Adding coordinates and distances to downtown Seattle and Bellevue (set E) lowers the median error to 8.6% for XGBoost and 11.1% for Ridge, against 10.2% and 12.2% for set C alone.

How held-out information is kept out

4.4 Leakage controls and scaling

The rules that keep every score honest, followed by the hold-out result.

  • Everything that learns from data is refit inside each fold. Imputer medians, scaling statistics, ZIP target encoding, the hot-ZIP flag and tier, and the outlier band are all learned inside one fitting function that is called separately for each cross-validation fold, so each fold learns them from its own training rows only.
  • Folds are grouped by property. 353 rows share a property id with another row; grouping keeps every property entirely in training or entirely in test.
  • Target encoding is cross-fitted. While the encoder is being fitted, each training row is encoded from folds that exclude it, so a row never sees its own price. Held-out rows are encoded with statistics from training rows only.
  • Held-out rows are never trimmed or labeled. The outlier band removes rows from fitting only. Test rows keep every outlier, and their prices never enter an encoding, a scaler, or a band.
  • Linear models are scaled, tree models are not. Ridge standardizes numeric inputs using the mean and spread of the training fold, because a penalty treats features on different scales unequally. XGBoost receives them unscaled because its splits depend only on the order of values.
  • The target transform lives inside the pipeline. The fitting function log-transforms the price and the prediction function applies the inverse (expm1) before scoring. It is the R counterpart of scikit-learn's TransformedTargetRegressor, so no metric is computed on a transformed scale by accident.
  • A hold-out set stays out of model selection. 4,328 sales (4,287 properties, chosen at random before any comparison) were set aside. The pipeline was chosen by cross-validation on the other 17,285 sales, then scored on the hold-out (the note under the hold-out table says how many times).

The pipeline uses XGBoost on feature set E with outlier trimming. It was chosen by the lowest cross-validated RMSE of log1p price on the development rows. On the 4,328 hold-out sales it reaches a median error of 8.5% against 34.4% for the median baseline, with 83.2% of predictions within 20% of the sale price, MAE $65,027 and RMSE $136,557. Dollar RMSE follows the largest sales, so read it with care: cross-validation gives $119,664 while the hold-out gives $136,557, and the largest sale is $7,062,500 in the development rows against $7,700,000 in the hold-out. The median error and the share within 20% are the steadier yardsticks.

Splits, cross-validation, metrics, and leakage control

5. Methodology

How the models are compared: the train and test splits, grouped cross-validation, the metrics, and the safeguards against leakage. Numbers come from scripts/run_models.R.

How the comparison is set up

5.1 Splits, cross-validation, and models

Every model uses feature set E from section 4.3 (C + coordinates and distance to downtown Seattle and Bellevue), with any ZIP encoding fitted inside each fold. Price is modeled as log1p(price) inside the fitting pipeline and predictions are inverted with expm1, so every metric is in US dollars on the original scale. Linear models receive scaled inputs and tree models do not. Outlier rows (price per square foot in the lowest or highest 1% of the training rows) are left out of fitting only. Cross-validation is 5-fold, grouped by property, repeated 3 times with the groups reshuffled, so each metric has 15 values reported as mean and standard deviation. The metrics are RMSE, MAE, R-squared, MAPE and median absolute error; train and predict times are recorded for each model. A time-based split is added as a second scenario because the file has a sale date.

ScenarioTraining rowsTest rowsHow the split is made
Random split17,2854,328Random 80/20 split by property id with random_state 42. It is the same split as the hold-out in section 4.4.
Time-based split17,2824,331The earliest sales (2014-05-02 to 2015-03-09) train and the latest (2015-03-10 to 2015-05-27) test, cut between calendar days. 90 test rows share a property id with a training row (a resale of a house sold earlier).

Models, all trained on the same inputs:

ModelFamilyInputs scaledHyperparameters
Linear regression (OLS)LinearyesNone
RidgeLinear, L2 penaltyyesPenalty strength chosen by 5-fold CV inside each fit
LassoLinear, L1 penaltyyesPenalty strength chosen by 5-fold CV inside each fit
Elastic netLinear, L1 + L2 penaltyyesStrength and L1 share chosen by 5-fold CV inside each fit
Random forestBagged treesnoFixed: 300 trees, at least 3 rows per leaf, half the features per split
Gradient boosting (gbm)BoostingnoFixed: 500 trees, depth 4, learning rate 0.05, 80% row sampling
XGBoostBoostingnoFixed: 500 trees, depth 4, learning rate 0.03

Metrics: RMSE, MAE, R-squared, MAPE and median absolute error, all in US dollars (formulas in the glossary), plus training and prediction time. The median error as a share of the price and the share of predictions within 20% are used in the feature-engineering and final-model sections.

Leakage control: everything that learns from data (imputation, scaling, ZIP encoding, the outlier band, hyperparameter search) is fitted on training rows only, folds are grouped by property so a house is never on both sides, and the test rows are used once at the end. The full list is in section 4.4.

Diagnostics on the test rows

8. Final model

The final model is the XGBoost with tuned settings and feature set E (C + coordinates and distance to downtown Seattle and Bellevue), refitted on all 17,285 training rows (16,939 after the outlier rule) and scored once on the test rows. Numbers come from scripts/run_final.R.

Where the model is accurate and where it is not

8.1 Diagnostics and residuals

On the 4,328 test sales the final XGBoost has a median error of 8.0% ($35,668 in dollars), with 84.5% of predictions within 20% of the sale price, against 34.4% for the median-price baseline. The median signed error is -0.3%, so the model is essentially unbiased overall. Error is not uniform: it is lowest in price decile 5 (6.8%) and highest in decile 1 (15.1%). The cheapest decile has a median signed error of +12.0% and the most expensive -7.2%, the usual pattern of a model that shrinks extremes toward the middle. 36 sales (0.8%) are off by more than 60% and are cut from the histogram, not from the scores.

Would more data help?

8.2 Learning curve

Test RMSE of log1p price falls from 0.186 with 1,695 training rows to 0.161 with all 16,939. The last step, from 14,396 to 16,939 rows, improves it by 0.6%, so the curve is close to flat: more rows of the same kind would help little, and gains must come from better features or other data. On the fitted rows the error is 0.125 against 0.161 on test rows, a moderate gap (a ratio of 1.28).

What drives the predictions

9. Model interpretation

Global feature importance and SHAP values for the tuned XGBoost model on the test rows.

Which inputs move the prediction

9.1 Feature importance and SHAP

SHAP splits each prediction into one additive contribution per feature, measured in log1p price units, so positive values raise the predicted price and negative values lower it. The top three features are zip_te (18.7%), sqft_living (14.6%), lat (11.3%) of the total mean absolute SHAP. Location features (ZIP encoding, coordinates and distances) together account for 43.9%, size features for 33.3%, and grade for 10.4%. Gain importance (orange diamonds) comes from the trees' split statistics and can rank features differently from SHAP because it favours features used in early splits. SHAP values were computed on the 4,328 test rows from the tuned XGBoost model; the contributions plus the baseline reproduce the model output to within 2.6e-05. The beeswarm shows 1,500 sampled test sales. Importance describes what the model uses, not what causes prices: correlated features such as the coordinates, the distances and the ZIP encoding share credit.

What the results cannot say

10. Limitations, risks, and next steps

Limits to keep in mind when using the numbers, and the changes most likely to improve them.

What these numbers cannot say

10.1 Limitations and risks

Each row names a limit and says what it means for the numbers in this report. Numbers in the rows are computed from the report's own results.

AreaLimitationWhat it means for the results
DataOne county and about 13 months. The sales run from 2 May 2014 to 27 May 2015, all in King County.The results describe this market in this period. They do not show how the model would do in another county, or in a market with different conditions.
Thin field documentation. Neither the file nor its OpenML description says when ratings such as grade, condition and view were assigned, how the neighbour areas (sqft_living15, sqft_lot15) were measured, or whether a sale was at market price.A field recorded after the sale could carry price information into the features, and a non-market sale (for example between relatives) can look like an unusually cheap sale. The report cannot rule either out; grade alone carries 10.4% of the model's attributions.
Few sales in the extreme groups. Only 163 of 21,613 sales (0.8%) are on the waterfront and 502 have grade 11 or higher.The least accurate groups on the test rows are waterfront homes (31 test sales, median error 23.7%), grade 5 (50 test sales, median error 16.4%), the cheapest price decile (433 test sales, median error 15.1%), against 8.0% overall. Scores for groups this small are imprecise, so differences between them should not be over-read.
ValidationThe headline error comes from a random split. The 8.0% median error is measured on test sales drawn at random from the whole period.On the time-based split (train on the earliest sales, test on the latest) the median absolute error of XGBoost with default settings rises from $38,130 to $45,327 (+19%), and by +8% on average for the linear models. Sales that come after the training period should therefore be expected to have a larger error than the headline. The later sales are somewhat harder even for the final model, which has seen that period: on the random split its median error is 8.9% for the 870 test sales after 10 March 2015 against 7.8% before, and its median signed error is -4.5% after against +1.1% before. The median price differs by +3.6% between the two periods. The report does not separate how much of the rise comes from the later period being harder and how much from the model not having seen it.
Folds are grouped by property, not by area. A house never appears in both training and test, but other homes from the same neighbourhood do.The scores describe valuing a home in an area that already has sales in the data, which is the usual case inside the county. They do not measure areas with no nearby sales, such as a new development or another county; location features carry 43.9% of the model's attributions, so that case matters. This has not been tested here.
The test rows are used in several sections. The same 4,328 test sales are scored in sections 4.4, 6.2, 7.3 and 8.1.Choices made by the pipeline (feature set, tuned settings, final model) use cross-validation on the training rows, not test scores, so selection has not inflated these numbers. Any change made after reading them would turn the test rows into validation data; a final unbiased estimate needs sales that no decision has seen, such as later months.
ModelingThe tuning budget is small and the ranges are fixed. Each tree model was given 20 random settings plus its default, all scored on the same folds.The best setting sits at the edge of the values tried for Random forest: mtry_frac = 0.3 (smallest tried); Gradient boosting (gbm): n.trees = 800 (largest tried), shrinkage = 0.08 (largest tried); XGBoost: nrounds = 800 (largest tried), min_child_weight = 1 (smallest tried), lambda = 0.5 (smallest tried), so a better setting may lie outside the ranges. Candidates within 0.5% of the best cross-validated score: Random forest 16 of 21; Gradient boosting (gbm) 2 of 21; XGBoost 3 of 21 (many means the model is insensitive to these settings; few means more search could still help). The chosen setting is the best of its group on the same folds that score it, so its cross-validated score is mildly optimistic; on the test rows the median error moves from 8.5% to 8.0% for XGBoost.
The model families are not compared like for like. Section 6.1 compares the trees at default settings and section 7.1 tunes them. Ridge, Lasso and Elastic net tune only their penalty, on inner folds that are not grouped by property (this touches the 1.6% of rows that are resales), and every linear model receives location only as the ZIP encoding and raw coordinates.With default settings the best linear model has a cross-validated median absolute error of $46,696 against $38,184 for the best tree model. The gap may reflect both the model class and the way features are supplied; the report does not test whether splines or interactions would close part of it.
The two best tuned models are close. XGBoost was chosen on cross-validated RMSE of log1p price; Gradient boosting (gbm) follows.They differ by 0.17 points of median error on the test rows (in favour of the chosen model) and by 1.2% in cross-validated RMSE. The 95% sampling interval for one model's median error is about +/- 0.28 points, so the test rows alone do not separate them and they should be treated as practically tied.
An outlier rule is applied everywhere. Rows whose price per square foot is in the lowest 1% or highest 1% of a fold's training rows are left out of fitting (346 of 17,285 training rows, 2.0%, in the final fit).The comparison in section 4.3 did not favour it: with feature set D the median error is 10.2% with the rule and 10.1% without for XGBoost, and 12.0% against 11.9% for Ridge. Only two models and one feature set were compared, and the rule was kept for all of them. Test rows are never trimmed, so the scores still cover every sale.
MeasurementScores are estimates from one sample. With 4,328 test sales the median error of 8.0% has a 95% bootstrap interval of 7.7% to 8.3%, and the share within 20% (84.5%) of 83.5% to 85.5%.The model returns one number per sale, and 16% of test sales are off by more than 20% and 36 by more than 60%, so a single estimate can miss by a wide margin; quote ranges rather than one figure. The interval is for one model; two models scored on the same sales are compared more precisely than it suggests, because their errors are correlated, but this report does not test such differences.
Dollar RMSE and R-squared follow a few sales. The final model's RMSE ($131,898) is 3.7 times its median absolute error ($35,668), and the largest test sale is $7,700,000.Squared errors let a handful of expensive sales dominate, and MAPE is inflated at the cheap end because it divides by the price. Use the median error and the share within 20% as the main measures, and RMSE and R-squared only to compare models on the same rows.
Timings depend on the machine. Times are wall-clock on one machine, with 4 threads for random forest and XGBoost; training time is one fit per fold or per model and prediction time is averaged over repeated calls.Differences of a fraction of a second are noise, and every time depends on the machine and on what else is running.
The model is described, not explained. SHAP values and importance show how the model uses its inputs, and the exploratory comparisons are associations in this sample.Correlated inputs (coordinates, distances to two centres, the ZIP encoding) share credit, and neither analysis shows that a feature causes a higher price, so a feature's share should not be read as a causal effect.

What to do next

10.2 Directions for improvement

Ordered by expected value for the effort, which is a judgement and not a measurement. Each row gives the evidence in this report that motivates it and a concrete way to check it.

PriorityDirectionWhy: evidence in this reportHow to check it
1Validate by area.Folds are grouped by property, not by area, and location features carry 43.9% of the model's attributions.Group the cross-validation folds by blocks of a coordinate grid, and by ZIP code, and compare the error with the current cross-validation. A large gap would show that the location features lean on nearby sales.
2Add time information and validate on later sales.On the time-based split (train on the earliest sales, test on the latest) the median absolute error of XGBoost with default settings rises from $38,130 to $45,327 (+19%), and by +8% on average for the linear models. The pipeline has no sale-date feature (age uses only the sale year); the final model's median signed error is -4.5% after 10 March 2015 against +1.1% before.Add the sale month or a local price index estimated from earlier sales only, score by rolling-origin validation (train on earlier months, test on the next), and add more years of sales if they can be had.
3Check the data fields.Neither the file nor its OpenML description says when ratings were assigned or whether a sale was at market price; grade carries 10.4% of the attributions.Ask the data owner for field definitions, refit without the rating fields (grade, condition, view) to see how much the score depends on them, and review the sales that sit far from their predicted price for non-market transfers.
4Improve the location features.Location features carry 43.9% of the attributions, and the least accurate groups are waterfront homes (31 test sales, median error 23.7%), grade 5 (50 test sales, median error 16.4%), the cheapest price decile (433 test sales, median error 15.1%).Add the median price per square foot of the nearest training sales (computed inside each fold, excluding the sale itself and other sales of the same property), distance to the shoreline, parks and transit, and school data. Keep a feature only if the grouped cross-validated error improves.
5Look at the price extremes.Median error is 15.1% in price decile 1 against 6.8% in decile 5; the cheapest decile has a median signed error of +12.0% and the most expensive -7.2%.Inspect the largest over-predictions among the cheapest sales; the 176 properties sold twice in the file show whether a very cheap sale was followed by a much higher resale, which would point to a non-market transfer. Then try recalibrating predictions with a monotone fit on out-of-fold predictions only, and check the decile table again.
6Give each estimate a range.16% of test sales are off by more than 20%, and 36 by more than 60%.Use conformal prediction or quantile regression, then check on the test rows that an 80% interval covers about 80% of sales, separately by price band.
7Combine models.The tuned Random forest, Gradient boosting (gbm) and XGBoost score within 0.6 points of each other on the test rows (8.0% to 8.6%), so none dominates; whether their errors differ enough for a blend to help has not been checked.Average, or stack, their out-of-fold predictions, and keep the blend only if the grouped cross-validated error improves by more than the fold-to-fold spread.
8Tune further, where it can pay.Tuning moved XGBoost's median error from 8.5% to 8.0%. Settings at the edge of the tried ranges: Random forest: mtry_frac = 0.3 (smallest tried); Gradient boosting (gbm): n.trees = 800 (largest tried), shrinkage = 0.08 (largest tried); XGBoost: nrounds = 800 (largest tried), min_child_weight = 1 (smallest tried), lambda = 0.5 (smallest tried).Extend only the ranges that bind (for example more trees with early stopping, or smaller regularisation), use repeated cross-validation so differences within the fold-to-fold spread are not chased, and stop when the top candidates tie.

Commands and downloads

11.2 How to reproduce, and the underlying files

Run the commands in this order from the project directory. Each script writes CSV files that the next one, and this report, read.

Rscript --vanilla scripts/run_features.R --output reports/latest
Rscript --vanilla scripts/run_models.R   --output reports/latest
Rscript --vanilla scripts/run_tuning.R   --output reports/latest
Rscript --vanilla scripts/run_final.R    --output reports/latest
Rscript --vanilla scripts/run_eda.R      --output reports/latest
Rscript tests/run_tests.R

The report is one HTML file: figures are embedded as images and the styles and scripts are inline, so it opens offline. Formulas in the glossary are typeset with KaTeX from a CDN when online; offline, the LaTeX source is shown instead. The same figures are also saved as PNG files in the figures directory.

These records describe sales made between May 2014 and May 2015. Positive extremes and repeat sales of the same property remain in the data; a few build and renovation years fall after the sale date. Group comparisons are descriptive.

Data: House Sales in King County, USA (OpenML dataset 42092), first published on Kaggle. The collection process is not documented there.
